lead: A class is a Python recipe for making objects. It groups data, called attributes, with actions, called methods. An object is one value built from that class. Each object keeps its own state while sharing the class's code. This idea exists because real programs handle many similar things: bank accounts, students, buttons, orders. You write the rules once in the class and create as many objects as needed. The example here is a BankAccount class with two objects, Asha and Ravi.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 variables and data types; Unit 2 functions and parameters.

blocks.text: A class is a template written with the keyword class. An object is a concrete value created by calling the class name, like BankAccount('Asha', 5000). The class says what every bank account has and can do; each object holds actual values.

Data stored on an object are attributes. Actions are methods. In BankAccount, bank_name = 'SBI' is a class attribute: one value shared by all accounts. holder and balance are instance attributes: each object has its own copy. Asha's balance and Ravi's balance are separate numbers.

__init__ is the setup method. Python runs it when a new object is created. It receives the new object as self and stores starting values. Full constructor details are in 4.2. For now, read __init__ as the place that gives each object its first state.
Some syllabi call this the blueprint and instance relationship. The class is the blueprint; an instance is one building made from it. The figure shows one class and two instances.
A method is a function defined inside a class. Its first parameter is self. When you call a1.deposit(1500), Python passes a1 as self and 1500 as amount. The method then changes a1.balance only.

def deposit(self, amount): followed by self.balance = self.balance + amount is correct. def deposit(amount): is wrong for an instance method: there is no self, so the object cannot be reached. Python may raise TypeError or treat amount as a local name. self is not a keyword; it is a normal parameter name, but every Python programmer uses self by convention.
Use dot notation to read or write attributes: a1.balance, a2.holder. To call a method, use parentheses: a1.deposit(1500). Writing a1.deposit without parentheses names the method but does not run it.

__str__ is a special method that returns a readable string for an object. print(a1) uses it. A simple version is return self.holder + ': ' + str(self.balance). This chapter previews it; related special methods appear in 4.6.

Rules for a simple class: use a Capitalised name, add a short docstring, list class attributes, write __init__ to set instance attributes, and give every instance method self first. Keep methods small.

sections.h3: Class attributes, instance attributes and lookup

blocks.text: Python looks up a1.bank_name in two places. First it checks the object's own attributes. If the name is not there, it checks the class. So a1.bank_name finds the shared 'SBI' from BankAccount.

If you assign a1.bank_name = 'HDFC', Python creates an instance attribute on a1. It does not change a2.bank_name and it does not change BankAccount.bank_name. This is a common exam point: assignment through an object creates or updates that object's attribute.

Instance attributes are for state that differs per object: holder, balance, roll number, cart items. Class attributes are for constants or defaults shared by all objects: bank name, minimum balance rule, category label.

Methods also live on the class. Two objects share the same method code, but each call binds self to a different object. That is why a1.deposit(1500) changes Asha's balance and a2 stays at 1200. Access control with private attributes is covered in 4.3.

figure.caption: The class holds the shared bank_name; each object holds its own holder and balance. Notice that after Asha deposits 1500, only her balance is 6500 while Ravi's remains 1200.

spec.title: Class to objects
spec.aria: A class BankAccount with class attribute bank_name SBI is the blueprint for two objects, Asha with balance 6500 and Ravi with balance 1200.

examples.question: Write a Python class BankAccount with a class attribute bank_name = 'SBI'. Its __init__ sets holder and balance. Define deposit(self, amount) that adds amount to balance. Create a1 = BankAccount('Asha', 5000) and a2 = BankAccount('Ravi', 1200). Call a1.deposit(1500). Print a1.balance, a2.balance and a1.bank_name. Show the exact output.
steps: Define class BankAccount: and set bank_name = 'SBI' in the class body. This is one shared class attribute.
Define __init__(self, holder, balance). Create a1: self is a1, holder is 'Asha', balance is 5000, so a1.balance starts at 5000.
Create a2: self is a2, holder is 'Ravi', balance is 1200, so a2.balance starts at 1200.
a2 is not involved in the call, so a2.balance stays at 1200.
a1.bank_name does not exist as an instance attribute, so Python reads the class attribute and gets 'SBI'.
examples.answer: The output is 6500, 1200 and SBI, so a1.balance is 6500, a2.balance is 1200 and a1.bank_name is SBI.
examples.check:
class BankAccount:
    bank_name = 'SBI'
    def __init__(self, holder, balance):
        self.holder = holder
        self.balance = balance
    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance = self.balance + amount

a1 = BankAccount('Asha', 5000)
a2 = BankAccount('Ravi', 1200)
a1.deposit(1500)
print(a1.balance)
print(a2.balance)

code.code:
class BankAccount:
    bank_name = 'SBI'

    def __init__(self, holder, balance):
        self.holder = holder
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance = self.balance + amount

    def __str__(self):
        return f'{self.holder}: {self.balance}'

a1 = BankAccount('Asha', 5000)
a2 = BankAccount('Ravi', 1200)
a1.deposit(1500)
print(a1.balance)
print(a2.balance)
print(a1.bank_name)

traps: Missing self: def deposit(amount): inside a class cannot reach the object. Every instance method takes self first; otherwise calls fail or variables stay local.
Calling BankAccount.deposit(1500) on the class skips the object, so self is missing. Call a1.deposit(1500).
Class attribute versus instance attribute: a1.bank_name = 'HDFC' creates an attribute on a1 only. It does not update a2 or the class.
Forgetting parentheses: a1.deposit gives a bound method, not a call. Use a1.deposit(1500).
Forgetting self. in __init__: balance = balance creates a local name; the object has no balance attribute.

quiz.q: What is an object in Python?
quiz.a: An object is a value created from a class. It has its own attributes and can call the class's methods.

quiz.q: Why does an instance method need self as its first parameter?
quiz.a: self receives the object on which the method is called. Through self, the method reads or changes that object's instance attributes.

quiz.q: A class has __init__(self, balance): self.balance = balance and deposit(self, amount): self.balance += amount. If a = Account(1000) and a.deposit(250), what is a.balance?
Asha and Ravi are two BankAccount objects. After a1.deposit(1500), why does a2.balance not change?
quiz.a: The call binds self to a1. The method changes a1.balance. a2 has its own separate balance attribute, so it stays unchanged.

quiz.q: Write a method withdraw(self, amount) that subtracts amount from balance.
State one difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute.
quiz.a: A class attribute is shared by all objects and is stored on the class. An instance attribute belongs to one object and is stored on that object.

quiz.q: What does __str__ do for an object?
quiz.a: __str__ returns a readable string for the object. print(object) uses that string.

beyond: Not for the exam. Python's dataclasses module writes common __init__, __str__ and comparison methods from attribute declarations, so simple classes need less code. Libraries such as attrs and Pydantic extend this idea with validation and typed fields. Web frameworks use classes to model database rows, and GUI toolkits use classes for widgets, so the same class-object split appears in production code. Search next for Python dataclasses, Pydantic models, and object-relational mapping models.
